mappings.note: MISFILED: the extract is the pankha passage from 'Winds of Change'. The sub-questions ask what 'significant cultural goods' implies, what the writer's attitude is, and what determined the variety -- evaluating supplied informative prose, C-3.1. No C-2.2 LO can be cited: this chapter's LOs are all about a poem, a character sketch or reported speech.

MISFILED content (the fan makers of 'Winds of Change'), but the task is a 'societal sketch' built from traits, challenges and triumphs the text shows -- the same operation as C-2.2-LO-18, applied to a community instead of one character. Cited on the operation, not the chapter.

MISFILED: how the pankha's shift from utility item to cultural good reflects the modern consumer. Evaluating a supplied text's implications, C-3.1. Not C-3.2: nothing is argued against, the passage's claim is unpacked.
MISFILED: the pankha etymology extract ('pankh' as feather, the Ajanta wall paintings) with inference and vocabulary sub-questions. Analysis of supplied informative material, C-3.1.
MISFILED: extract on celebrating pankhas, asking what the author implies by 'celebrate' and what workshops achieve. Inference from supplied prose, C-3.1.
MISFILED: how appreciating the stories behind the crafts affects craftspersons. A short inference from the same foreign passage, C-3.1.

MISFILED: the ultimate message of 'Winds of Change' about India's artistic heritage. Summarising a supplied text's argument, C-3.1. C-4.3 was considered and rejected -- it concerns the role of LANGUAGE in identity, not crafts.
MISFILED: the central theme of 'Winds of Change' and the pankha as a figure for craft resilience. Evaluating a supplied text as a whole, C-3.1.

Write a DIARY ENTRY as an elderly Rajasthan artisan about how demand for his craft has changed -- first person, events plus the writer's response to them, which is C-1.3-LO-4 word for word. The subject matter is borrowed from 'Winds of Change' but the task type is exactly this chapter's diary outcome. DEFECT: concept tag 'Diary Entry' is right while the content belongs to another chapter.

Write a SPEECH for a school assembly urging support for artisans. C-1.3 names speeches among real-life writing situations, but neither of this chapter's two C-1.3 LOs fits -- LO-3 is an article, LO-4 a diary entry -- so the citation stops at the competency. DEFECT: concept tag reads 'Direct and Indirect Speech', which is a grammar tag on a composition task.

Write a LETTER to a friend describing a workshop you attended and what you learned. Writing from one's own experience in a descriptive style, C-1.2. Not C-1.3-LO-3: an informal letter is not an article with opening, middle and close. DEFECT: the answer breaks off mid-sentence and continues with 'Vitamin-M' story text -- '...workshop that NODIA PAGE 368 ... decides to step out to buy a Tamil newspaper, Ravi follows him closely...'.

Complete a graphic organiser from your experience with an elderly person, then DISCUSS the points with classmates and teacher. The discussion-to-conclusion form is C-1.1. Not C-1.2: the written output is organiser notes, and the assessed act is the discussion. DEFECT: concept tag 'Intonation in Questions' is unrelated.

Think of a tradition, story or recipe passed down by a grandparent, say what it means to you and how it connects to your growing-up years. Personal narrative from own experience, C-1.2. Not C-2.1-LO-8, which needs this text set against other writing about growing old. DEFECT: the stem opens with a stray glossary line, 'winced pain made a slight movement showing pain or discomfort'.

'Was Grandpa lost as feared by Ravi's mother?' -- plot-level comprehension of the story. This chapter has no LO for plot recall (LO-15 to LO-17 are poem outcomes, LO-18 is a character sketch, LO-19 is grammar), so C-2.2 competency. DEFECT: the stem begins mid-sentence, 'bus stop and boards the first bus'.

'How would Ravi feel after seeing Grandpa?' -- the text never states it, so the answer must be inferred from what he does (the hug, the relief). That is C-2.2-LO-18, building the character from what is shown rather than stated. DEFECT: the stem carries the whole of the previous question and its model answer before the real prompt.

The extract has Grandpa longing for the brick house and the mango tree; sub-question i asks which emotion he displays (nostalgic, not regretful or apologetic) and the rest ask why he hated the city and why he came anyway. Reading the man from what he says, C-2.2-LO-18. C-2.2-LO-15 was rejected: its sensory imagery is 'in the poem', and this is prose. DEFECT: concept tag 'Prepositions of Place and Direction' does not match.

Identify the tone of Grandpa's reply (calm), why Ravi is confused and embarrassed, why the mother is impatient -- three characters read off their words and behaviour. C-2.2-LO-18. Not C-2.2-LO-19: reported speech is not being converted, only interpreted.

A guided personal account of caring for an older person, written to sentence prompts. Writing from one's own experience, C-1.2. Not C-1.3-LO-3: no article structure is asked for. DEFECT: the stem is only the tail of a prompt -- 'Caring for them deepened my understanding of the ageing process, particularly...' -- with the instruction missing.

The answer is a finished article -- 'Our Inspiring Elderly, By XYZ, Grade 9' -- with an opening, a developed middle and a close, which is C-1.3-LO-3 exactly, and the concept tag 'Article Writing' agrees. DEFECT: the stem is not the article prompt at all; it is the previous item's model answer pasted in, so the actual instruction has been lost.

A gap-fill using the story's movement and sound words (ducked, darted, crawl, thudded, whirr, shrieks). C-2.2-LO-15 would be the natural home, but that LO is written as 'sensory imagery in the POEM' and this is the prose story, so the citation stops at C-2.2. Not LO-19, which is reported speech and prepositions. Reported as a frame gap. DEFECT: the stem is a fragment starting at blank 6.

Fill in prepositions -- through, over, near, in, along, towards -- after a definition anchored on 'Ravi took position behind a big banyan'. The prepositions-of-place-and-direction half of C-2.2-LO-19. Not LO-18: no character is being built.

Classify sentences as Wh- or Yes/No interrogatives. A grammar drill, but C-2.2-LO-19 covers only direct-to-indirect speech and prepositions, so interrogative types have no LO here -- C-2.2 competency. Reported as a frame gap.

Convert a conversation into reported speech -- 'Arvind asked Priya if she ... replied in the affirmative ... further enquired ...'. The direct-and-indirect-speech half of C-2.2-LO-19. DEFECT: the stem is a fragment beginning at blank 4, so the source conversation is missing and only the answer reveals what was asked.

A gap-fill answered from a listening transcript ('Meditating on a daily basis is beneficial in comfortably tackling ...'). C-3.1 is the only competency that names AUDIO material alongside written. DEFECT: both the transcript and the answer key are missing -- the answer field is just the lead-in 'Here are the correct answers based on the given transcript:'.

A speaking activity on intonation -- falling for Wh- questions, rising for Yes/No and for tag questions. Oral language used appropriately in context, C-1.1. Not C-1.4 (scripting with technology) and not C-2.2-LO-19, which is written conversion. DEFECT: the answer states 'No written answer required', so the item is unmarkable as stored.

Give two pieces of EVIDENCE to disprove the claim that Grandpa's memory is failing. C-2.2-LO-18 is the only outcome that asks for the character to be built from evidence rather than assertion, and this item demands the evidence explicitly. Not C-3.2: the premises are not being weighed, the text is being cited.
Two characteristic traits each for Grandfather, Ravi and Ravi's mother -- character sketching, C-2.2-LO-18.

Why Ravi worried about what Grandpa had at the tea stall -- recall of the banned items and the reason for them. Plot comprehension with no LO available, so C-2.2 competency. Not LO-18: nothing about Ravi's character is asked.

'Do you think it was easy for Ravi to follow his Grandfather? If yes why, if no why not' -- a position that must be defended from the text's incidents. The yes/no-plus-reason form is C-3.2, argument with rationale. Not C-2.2-LO-18: the question is about the difficulty of the task, not about who Ravi is.

Give one argument FOR and one AGAINST 'Ravi is a good detective'. Weighing premises on both sides is C-3.2 at its most literal. Chosen over C-2.2-LO-18 because the item requires a balanced argument, not a sketch.
Was Grandfather aware he was being followed, and HOW DO YOU KNOW -- the detective book, the remark about trailing a suspect, the twinkle, the swapped cap. Inference plus cited evidence, C-2.2-LO-18.

'Who needs Vitamin-M, and why' turns on reading the title as a figure and supporting the reading from the text -- the mother, who forgot her own father's birthday. That is C-2.2-LO-17, interpreting the central symbol with textual support. NOTE: LO-17 is worded 'of the poem' while the text here is a prose story; I cite it on substance and flag the wording as a frame mismatch, since no other outcome covers the title symbol.
Give an example of age-based discrimination you have experienced or observed. Writing from one's own experience, C-1.2. Not C-3.2: no premise is being evaluated, an instance is being supplied.

Points the reader at other stories about caring for family members across ages, naming Mulk Raj Anand's 'The Lost Child' to read and discuss. Setting this text beside other writing on ageing and family is C-2.1-LO-8. DEFECTS: the stem is fused with the tail of an earlier answer ('Why is it memorable for you? It is memorable because...'), the answer says there are no direct textual questions, and an advert, 'Click Here to Buy book on Amazon', sits inside it.

Extract on why Grandpa moved in -- the double dose, getting lost. The sub-questions ask what prompted the move and judge statements about his intent, i.e. what the text shows about him. C-2.2-LO-18. Not C-2.1-LO-8, which needs a comparison with other writing about growing old; none is offered here.

'I'll have you know, Vidya...' -- which DOMINANT CHARACTER TRAIT the speech shows (fierce independence, not resigned helplessness). A character read straight off the evidence, C-2.2-LO-18, and the concept tag 'Character Analysis' agrees.
Who gives Ravi the secret mission -- plot recall. No LO covers plot in this chapter, so C-2.2 competency.
What Grandpa steps out to buy (a Tamil newspaper) -- plot detail, C-2.2 competency.
Ravi follows while pretending to be a secret detective -- plot detail, C-2.2 competency. Not LO-18: the pretence is stated in the text, not inferred.

Which statement about the morning walk is correct -- 'a fun, independent stroll' against 'sad and slow' or 'got lost'. The options are competing readings of Grandpa's character, so C-2.2-LO-18 rather than plain recall.
Grandpa's first stop (a children's park) -- plot detail, C-2.2 competency.
The snack at the park (roasted peanuts) -- plot detail, C-2.2 competency.
What the snack was wrapped in (a paper-cone) -- plot detail, C-2.2 competency.
What Grandpa watched at the park (the playing children) -- plot detail, C-2.2 competency.
Where he stopped after the park (a roadside tea stall) -- plot detail, C-2.2 competency.
What kind of tea he drank (sweet, sugary) -- plot detail, C-2.2 competency.
How many bananas (two) -- plot detail, C-2.2 competency.
The other banned item (a cold ice cream) -- plot detail, C-2.2 competency.
Where Grandpa recently moved (a bustling city) -- setting recall, C-2.2 competency.
Who he lives with (daughter and grandson) -- plot detail, C-2.2 competency.
The grandson's name (Ravi) -- plot detail, C-2.2 competency.
The structure he missed (a small brick house) -- recall of the detail, C-2.2 competency. Not LO-18: the item asks what, not what it reveals.
The tree he missed most (a big mango tree) -- plot detail, C-2.2 competency.
Why living alone was no longer safe (he slipped and fell in the garden) -- plot detail, C-2.2 competency.

Which incident showed failing memory (taking a double dose) -- recall. C-2.1-LO-8 was rejected: it requires this treatment of memory to be set against OTHER writing about growing old, which the item does not ask.
What else he forgot (his way home) -- plot detail, C-2.2 competency.
How Ravi's mother SPEAKS to Grandpa -- loud and patronising. Manner of speech as evidence of character, C-2.2-LO-18, not bare recall.
How Grandpa felt about his daughter's rules -- 'like a prisoner'. The figure is his, and the item asks the reader to register what it shows about his position: C-2.2-LO-18.

Why Ravi feels guilty -- because he sees Grandpa reduced to a prisoner by his mother's tone. An inference about one character drawn from another's behaviour, C-2.2-LO-18. DEFECT: the answer field trails page furniture and two orphan options, 'NODIA PAGE 382 CBSE CLASS 9 ENGLISH R1 (c) Talking quite softly (d) Laughing out happily'.

What Ravi did when he found Grandpa safe (gave him a warm hug) -- plot detail, C-2.2 competency. The inference version of this same moment appears earlier in the chapter and is mapped to LO-18; this one asks only what happened.
